description:
We are Team Astrix, a team passionate about space technology, Earth observation, data analysis, and building practical solutions to real-world challenges.

Our project, FireSync, brings satellite fire observations into one interactive platform. It helps users explore global fire activity, investigate specific regions, compare observations from different satellite sensors, and trace each detection back to its source.
summary:
FireSync is an interactive web platform that brings NASA FIRMS active-fire observations into one place, making it easier to explore fire activity and understand how different satellite sensors observe it. Users can explore a global fire map, investigate specific regions, view detection statistics, compare observations from MODIS and VIIRS, and inspect individual detection records alongside the methodology and limitations behind the data.

The project addresses the challenge of making satellite fire observations easier to explore and interpret. Different sensors have different spatial resolutions and observation times, so their records do not always tell exactly the same story. FireSync helps users examine these differences through interactive maps and comparisons, while keeping the underlying observations and their limitations visible.

Understanding these observations matters because informed interpretation of satellite data can support awareness, research, and better understanding of fire activity on Earth.
details:
FireSync is an interactive web platform designed to make NASA FIRMS active-fire satellite observations easier to explore, compare, and understand.

The platform brings fire-detection records from different satellite sensors into one interface. Users can explore a global map of detected fire activity, select an area of interest, view regional statistics, compare observations from MODIS and VIIRS, and inspect individual detection records. It also provides information about the methodology and limitations of the data, helping users understand what satellite observations can—and cannot—tell them.

FireSync offers several benefits: it makes large collections of satellite observations more accessible, helps users investigate regional fire activity, and makes differences between satellite sensors easier to examine. For example, MODIS and VIIRS have different spatial resolutions and observation times. Comparing their observations can reveal differences in coverage and detection patterns, rather than assuming that every sensor observes the same events in exactly the same way.

Our project’s creative approach is to bring exploration, regional analysis, sensor comparison, and individual-record inspection together in a single interactive experience. Instead of presenting hotspot counts alone, FireSync encourages users to investigate the evidence behind the numbers.

During development, our team considered data accessibility, map usability, sensor differences, observation timing, spatial resolution, and scientific limitations. We also considered the importance of avoiding misleading conclusions: a satellite detection does not necessarily represent a unique fire, and the absence of a detection does not prove that no fire exists.

We used NASA FIRMS data, Python for backend development and data processing, web technologies for the interactive frontend, and Git/GitHub for version control and project collaboration. AI-assisted tools, including ChatGPT, Claude, and Manus, supported parts of our planning, development workflow, and project preparation.

Our intended impact is to help people explore satellite-based fire observations more clearly and critically, supporting greater awareness and understanding of fire activity on Earth.
